# Detecting mixed-state order in the laboratory {#sec-experiments}

An order parameter is useful only when its relation to a measurement is understood. For ordinary SSB, one measures a spin or density correlation repeatedly and averages the outcomes. A nonlinear function of $\rho$ requires a different resource: multiple copies, a particular purification, a tractable model, or a sufficiently small subsystem for tomography. This chapter derives those options and explains how the first experimental platforms used them.

The evidence reviewed here is restricted to work publicly available by **22 October 2026**. The cold-atom and superconducting-device results are described with their finite-size and modeling assumptions. Their existence does not turn arbitrary mixed-state fidelity into an efficiently measurable observable.

## Why one expectation value is insufficient

Every fixed measurement outcome probability has the form $\operatorname{Tr}(M\rho)$ and is linear in $\rho$. If two ensembles have the same density matrix, no measurement on one copy can determine which ensemble decomposition was used. Conversely, a nonlinear diagnostic is not the expectation of a fixed operator on one copy for all $\rho$.

This does not forbid estimating a nonlinear quantity from many repetitions. Tomography estimates $\rho$ and then computes the quantity classically. The difficulty is scaling: an arbitrary $N$-qubit density matrix has $4^N-1$ real parameters. The purpose of specialized protocols is to exploit more structure than arbitrary tomography allows.

For a unitary probe $A$, the Rényi-2 numerator and purity can be measured using two copies. The swap identity is

$$
\operatorname{Tr}[S(X\otimes Y)]=\operatorname{Tr}(XY),
$$ {#eq-exp-swap}

where $S|a\rangle|b\rangle=|b\rangle|a\rangle$. Therefore

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A\rho A^\dagger)
=\operatorname{Tr}\big[S(\rho\otimes A\rho A^\dagger)\big],\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)=\operatorname{Tr}[S(\rho\otimes\rho)].
$$ {#eq-exp-two-copy}

One may use a controlled-swap circuit, or local interference/Bell-basis measurements whose product measures the global swap. For qubits, a single-site swap is $(I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z)/2$. Joint-copy protocols trade circuit complexity for direct access to quadratic quantities.

The denominator cannot be ignored. If purity is exponentially small, an additive error that is tiny on a scale of one can still overwhelm the normalized ratio. For instance, a swap outcome with variance of order one needs order $\epsilon^{-2}$ shots for additive precision $\epsilon$. Resolving a quantity of order $2^{-N}$ by such a generic estimator can require exponentially many repetitions.

## Randomized measurements and their statistical cost

Two physical copies need not coexist. One can measure independent preparations in randomly selected local Pauli bases. For one qubit, an unbiased density-matrix estimator from basis $U$ and outcome $b$ is

$$
\widehat\rho=3U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U-I.
$$

Tensor products give an $N$-qubit estimator with $\mathbb E\widehat\rho=\rho$. Independent snapshots then satisfy
$\mathbb E\operatorname{Tr}(\widehat\rho\widehat\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)$.
Take $\sigma=A\rho A^\dagger$ and estimate the numerator and denominator separately. The resulting finite-sample ratio is generally biased even though each quadratic estimator is unbiased; resampling or bias analysis is needed for quantitative error bars.

@sun2025randomized develops this route specifically for SW-SSB diagnostics and demonstrates it numerically for decohered Ising chains. Randomization provides an implementable measurement scheme, but does not remove the growth of variance for global nonlinear observables. Restricting to a region can make tomography or randomized estimates feasible, at the cost of replacing a global diagnostic with a local one.

## Canonical purification is a measurement resource

If a device can prepare

$$
|\sqrt\rho\rangle\!\rangle=\sum_{a,b}(\sqrt\rho)_{ab}|a\rangle_L|b\rangle_R,
$$

the Rényi-1 correlator becomes an ordinary doubled-state expectation:

$$
R_1(A)=\langle\!\langle\sqrt\rho|A\otimes A^*|\sqrt\rho\rangle\!\rangle.
$$ {#eq-exp-canonical}

For a two-point charged probe, this is a two-point function of local inter-copy operators. @weinstein2025 identifies this route to scalable detection for families whose canonical purifications have efficient preparations.

Preparing *some* purification is not sufficient. If $|\Psi\rangle=(I\otimes V)|\sqrt\rho\rangle\!\rangle$, then the right-copy operator must be transformed by $V$ to obtain @eq-exp-canonical. That operator may become nonlocal or unknown. The resource is a controlled canonical purification or an equivalent preparation with a known, tractable environment operator.

Local formulations offer another compromise. Estimate $F(\rho_A,O\rho_AO^\dagger)$ in regions of increasing radius around a charged insertion. The region size controls both the physical approximation and the measurement cost. If the required resources grow exponentially with region volume $v$, a budget polynomial in total system size can reach $v=O(\log N)$. @divi2026local develops this strategy; @liu2026local gives an infinite-volume local formulation. Global order implies suitable local fidelity order, but the converse needs additional hypotheses. Pure locally thermal states provide a warning against replacing every global definition by a finite-region test.

If a matrix-product density-operator representation is available, variational sequential circuits can give certified lower and upper fidelity bounds [@liu2026certification]. This is valuable for one-dimensional numerical studies. Its efficiency presumes an economical representation and successful optimization; it is not a promise that arbitrary laboratory states have such a representation.

## What the hardness theorem does and does not say

@feng2025hardness constructs efficiently preparable ensembles without SW-SSB that are computationally indistinguishable from ensembles with it, under the paper's pseudorandomness assumptions. This rules out a universally efficient, state-agnostic detection algorithm with the stated experimental access. It does not prohibit efficient diagnostics for thermal states, known channels, Gaussian states, canonical purifications, or other structured families.

The distinction can be phrased as a resource table:

| Access supplied | Quantity obtained | Principal limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Arbitrary copies and global swap | $R_2$ numerator and purity | Small purity and global-measurement variance |
| Random local measurements | Quadratic overlaps | Snapshot variance and ratio bias |
| Canonical purification | $R_1$ as an ordinary correlator | Preparation and copy-basis control |
| Local tomography | Reduced-state fidelity | Region-size cost; local/global distinction |
| Known pure input and dephasing kernel | Fidelity and $R_2$ for compatible probes | Input-purity and channel assumptions; shot cost |
| Samples plus a learned probability model | Diagonal-state $R_1,R_2$ estimators | Model bias and support errors |

A successful experiment should explain which row it uses. The following platforms use different rows.

## Dephased Fermi gas: turning snapshots into nonlinear correlations

Occupation imaging completely dephases the measured state in the number basis. If a configuration is $\boldsymbol n$, the resulting diagonal density matrix has weights $p_{\boldsymbol n}$. For a transfer from $j$ to $i$, let $\boldsymbol n'$ be the allowed displaced configuration. Then

$$
R_1(i,j)=\sum_{\boldsymbol n}\sqrt{p_{\boldsymbol n}p_{\boldsymbol n'}},\qquad
R_2(i,j)=\frac{\sum_{\boldsymbol n}p_{\boldsymbol n}p_{\boldsymbol n'}}{\sum_{\boldsymbol n}p_{\boldsymbol n}^2}.
$$ {#eq-exp-diagonal}

Disallowed transfers contribute zero. For a diagonal state and a compatible one-to-one charge move, the root-fidelity expression has the same classical square-root-overlap structure, with the appropriate subnormalized support for a nonunitary hopping probe. Fermionic hopping signs cancel between the two matrix elements in these nonlinear expressions.

Direct frequency estimation of all $p_{\boldsymbol n}$ remains exponentially expensive. Suppose, however, a classical model supplies probabilities $q_{\boldsymbol n}$. Experimental samples $\boldsymbol n_m\sim p$ give

$$
\widehat R_{1,\mathrm{QC}}=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M
\sqrt{\frac{q_{\boldsymbol n'_m}}{q_{\boldsymbol n_m}}},\qquad
\widehat R_{2,\mathrm{QC}}=
\frac{\sum_mq_{\boldsymbol n'_m}}{\sum_mq_{\boldsymbol n_m}}.
$$ {#eq-exp-qc}

If $q=p$, taking the sampling expectation reproduces @eq-exp-diagonal. If $q\ne p$, more shots remove sampling error but leave model bias. This distinction is essential: a smooth model can assign probability to a transferred partner that is actually absent from the true support, artificially raising an overlap. Validation must therefore probe the model assumptions as well as statistical convergence.

The cold-atom experiment of @wang2026fermi uses a learned Gaussian fermionic reference because its weakly interacting gas is close to a number-conserving free-fermion state. Such a state is determined by its one-body correlation matrix $G$. To see why this helps, diagonalize the single-particle density matrix; the normal modes are independent Bernoulli occupations. In a nonsingular mixed Gaussian state, the probability for exactly the sites $S$ to be occupied can be written

$$
q(S)=\det(I-G)\det\big([G(I-G)^{-1}]_S\big).
$$ {#eq-exp-gaussian-probability}

This determinant formula follows from the Gaussian operator representation $\rho=\det(I-G)\exp[c^\dagger\log(G(I-G)^{-1})c]$. Singular pure-state limits are obtained continuously; a fixed-number Slater determinant instead gives configuration weights as squared orbital determinants. These polynomial calculations replace an exponentially large table of probabilities by a matrix model. The fitted $G$ minimizes the empirical negative log likelihood, equivalently the data-to-model KL divergence up to a data-only constant.

The experiment loads $^6$Li into a square optical lattice, images one spin component, and analyzes a dephased effectively single-component gas. The full homogeneous system has approximately $14\times14$ sites; central subsystems are used to assess size dependence. It finds nondecaying nonlinear correlations in the dephased metallic regime. A commensurate superlattice drives a metal-to-insulator change in the underlying state, accompanied by suppression of the nonlinear order after dephasing. The paper compares quantum-classical estimates with correlators evaluated entirely in the learned reference, and studies subsystem condensate densities.

A useful finite-size statistic is

$$
\varrho_1(L)=\frac1{V_L^2}\sum_{i,j\in A_L}R_1(i,j).
$$ {#eq-exp-condensate}

If $R_1\to r_\infty>0$, the double sum has leading term $r_\infty V_L^2$. Short-range contributions are only of order $V_L$, so $\varrho_1\to r_\infty$. If $R_1$ decays with a finite correlation length, $\varrho_1$ instead vanishes as $1/V_L$ away from boundary corrections. Algebraic order gives a different, size-dependent power. This diagnostic avoids choosing just one separation, although nearby-site contributions and fit windows still matter.

At nonzero temperature, fixed-sector thermal states can already have nonlinear order on both metallic and insulating sides. Thus the ideal zero-temperature transition, the dephasing enhancement, and a finite-temperature experimental crossover should be separated. A finite subsystem is also not itself an exactly fixed-charge system, because it exchanges particles with its complement. The probability-based correlators remain meaningful, but interpreting them as bulk phase diagnostics uses a thermodynamic argument in addition to the estimator.

## A five-qubit cluster array: the role of discarded records

The superconducting-array experiment of @cao2026mixed prepares a five-qubit cluster state and contrasts selective dephasing, conditioned measurements, and discarded records. Its simplest ideal reduced state follows directly from cluster stabilizers. Trace out even sites 2 and 4. All stabilizer products with support on those sites vanish under the trace, leaving

$$
\rho_{1,3,5}=\frac18(I+X_1X_3X_5).
$$ {#eq-exp-three-parity}

It is the maximally mixed positive-parity state of three qubits. Its ordinary $Z_iZ_j$ expectations vanish, while $Z_iZ_j$ commutes with the parity and leaves $\rho$ unchanged. The root fidelity is therefore one. Conditioned on measurements of the even sublattice, the odd sites can instead form GHZ-like states with outcome-dependent correlation signs. Averaging discards the signs and removes the ordinary correlation while retaining the nonlinear overlap.

This gives an exact consistency check: measuring the discarded subsystem in a different complete basis cannot change the unconditioned reduced density matrix. It can change the conditioned decomposition and the amount of visible trajectory order. A basis-dependent averaged state would indicate retained postselection, incomplete averaging, or an experimental imperfection.

The reported experiment uses full few-qubit tomography and also symmetry resolution. The unprojected reduced state has appreciable leakage between parity sectors; projecting the tomographic estimate with $P_+=(I+X_1X_3X_5)/2$ produces a symmetry-resolved state. Such a projection is an analysis operation with a specified selection probability. The observations are therefore finite-size demonstrations of the diagnostic structure and mixed-SPT mechanisms, not a thermodynamic extrapolation from a three-site system.

## Processor transitions using a known-channel kernel

The work of @wei2026processor, submitted on 19 October 2026, studies matrix-product initial states under long-range pair dephasing. It reports finite-size crossings and scaling collapses for chains with $N=6,9,12$, together with decaying ordinary correlations. Its reconstruction protocol is especially instructive because it makes the extra prior information explicit.

Let the initial state be pure, $|\psi\rangle$, and let pair errors $Z_kZ_l$ occur independently with known probabilities $p_{kl}$. Their net action is $Z(\boldsymbol s)=\prod_iZ_i^{s_i}$ with even parity. Instead of enumerating all error masks, form their characteristic kernel

$$
\mathcal K(\boldsymbol w)=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol s}(-1)^{\boldsymbol s\cdot\boldsymbol w}
=\prod_{k<l:\,w_k\ne w_l}(1-2p_{kl}).
$$ {#eq-exp-channel-kernel}

For each pair, the random sign is nontrivial only when $w_k\ne w_l$; independence turns the expectation into a product. This derives the kernel using $O(N^2)$ arithmetic, without computing the full distribution of masks.

Write the input amplitudes as $e^{i\phi_z}\sqrt{P_z}$. After dephasing,

$$
\rho_{zz'}=e^{i(\phi_z-\phi_{z'})}\sqrt{P_zP_{z'}}\,\mathcal K(z\oplus z').
$$ {#eq-exp-kernel-density}

For a probe $A=Z_iZ_j$, the diagonal input-phase unitary commutes with both channel and probe. Common-unitary invariance of fidelity removes it. Consequently computational-basis samples from the input contain all the unknown state information needed for this particular reconstruction. The conclusion fails for arbitrary mixed inputs: two mixed density matrices can share $P_z$ but have different off-diagonal structure and different fidelity correlators.

The Rényi-2 identity follows immediately by multiplying matrix elements:

$$
R_2(i,j)=\frac{\mathbb E_{z,z'}[d(z)d(z')\mathcal K(z\oplus z')^2]}
{\mathbb E_{z,z'}[\mathcal K(z\oplus z')^2]},\qquad
d(z)=(-1)^{z_i+z_j}.
$$ {#eq-exp-kernel-r2}

The denominator is purity. Independent sample pairs should exclude a shot paired with itself when estimating the quadratic averages.

Fidelity can be reconstructed with a Gram matrix. For $M$ measured inputs $z_a$, define

$$
G_{ab}=\frac{\mathcal K(z_a\oplus z_b)}M,\qquad
D_{ab}=\delta_{ab}d(z_a).
$$

Factoring the channel density matrix into error-ensemble vectors shows that the nonzero eigenvalues of the empirical probe-weighted operator equal those of $G^{1/2}DG^{1/2}$. Taking the trace norm yields

$$
\widehat F=\left\|G^{1/2}DG^{1/2}\right\|_1.
$$ {#eq-exp-gram-fidelity}

This shifts a potentially exponential Hilbert-space calculation to an $M\times M$ matrix calculation. Its dense classical cost scales as $O(N^2M^2+M^3)$. That statement is polynomial in the *number of supplied shots*; it does not prove a polynomial number of shots for fixed precision across all states and channels. The nonlinear estimator can also have finite-shot bias.

Computational-basis measurements reconstruct the ordinary, fidelity, and Rényi-2 correlators. A second Hadamard-test setting accesses off-diagonal string expectations. The protocol evaluates a known target channel by classical processing of input data, so channel correctness and input purity are substantive assumptions. It is a different task from blind tomography of an unknown noisy output. The experiment explicitly distinguishes fidelity and Rényi-2 transition estimates; their agreement is not imposed as a universal identity.

## Reading finite-size evidence responsibly

A thermodynamic phase is defined by a limit, while every device is finite. A nonzero correlator at one separation establishes an overlap, not spontaneous symmetry breaking by itself. Increasing the separation with size, testing ordinary correlator decay, and comparing alternative finite-size fits make the interpretation stronger.

For a conventional continuous transition a common ansatz is
$R(L,p)=L^{-2\Delta}\mathcal F((p-p_c)L^{1/\nu})$.
Crossings of $L^{2\Delta}R$ can estimate $p_c$, but the scaling dimension and correlation-length exponent are fitted parameters and may be effective over a narrow size window. BKT transitions have exponentially diverging lengths, $\xi\sim\exp[b/\sqrt{|p-p_c|}]$, so a simple power-law collapse may misidentify the asymptotic behavior. Hardware errors, symmetry leakage, boundary conditions, and estimator bias can imitate rounding or shift apparent crossings.

The most convincing conclusion through the cutoff is that nonlinear mixed-state order has become experimentally accessible with well-specified resources. The next stage is to enlarge scaling windows, certify model assumptions, and design observables that remain economical as entropy and system size increase.

## Worked exercises

### An incorrect learned model

Let the true distribution be concentrated on $|01\rangle$, and consider the hop between sites 1 and 2. A model assigns equal probabilities to $01$ and $10$. Compare true $R_1$ and the infinite-data quantum-classical estimator.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The transferred partner $10$ has true probability zero, so the true overlap is zero. Every observed sample is $01$, but the model ratio is one, so @eq-exp-qc returns one. Sampling more accurately cannot repair this support error. Prior knowledge and validation of the learned distribution are part of the measurement protocol.
:::

### The kernel at zero and maximal pair noise

For a connected graph of pair channels with $p_{kl}=1/2$ on every graph edge, which masks $w$ have $\mathcal K(w)\ne0$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every edge crossing between $w=0$ and $w=1$ contributes a zero factor. A nonzero kernel therefore requires $w$ constant on each connected component. For a connected graph only the all-zero and all-one masks survive, with kernel one. This retains the global parity constraint while removing other computational-basis coherences.
:::

### Purity and error bars

Suppose numerator and purity both equal $10^{-4}$, each with additive uncertainty $10^{-5}$. Estimate the uncertainty of their ratio if the estimates are independent.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Linear propagation gives relative variance $(10^{-5}/10^{-4})^2+(10^{-5}/10^{-4})^2=0.02$, so the ratio has uncertainty about $0.14$ around one. A seemingly small absolute uncertainty does not give a precise normalized correlator. Correlated estimators can improve or worsen this estimate and require their covariance in the propagation.
:::
